title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 138 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 658–660 (Night 138, continuing directly from nights-137), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 138 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The Great Chamberlain, now sultan in Baghdad, tells his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān to treat her dead brother's widow with honour. The story turns to the next generation: Kān Mā Kān, son of Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and his cousin Qaḍā Fakān, Sharrukān's daughter, grow up and reach fifteen, and each is praised in verse. On a feast day Kān Mā Kān follows her and recites a love poem; she is furious, threatens to complain of him to the Chamberlain, and he goes home in anger. Her mother hushes the matter for fear the Sultan will hear of it, but the love is soon the talk of Baghdad's women, and the night ends as Kān Mā Kān, afraid of her anger, speaks his longing in verse. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirty-eighth night,
sentences.n: The small alif over the lām of thalāthūn is the print's own: it spells the word without its long alif (والثلٰثون).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْحَاجِبَ لَمَّا أَخْبَرَتْهُ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ بِخَبَرِ زَوْجَةِ أَخِيهَا قَالَ لَهَا أَكْرِمِي مَثْوَاهَا وَأَغْنِي فَقْرَهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ḥājiba lammā akhbarathu nuzhatu al-zamāni bi-khabari zawjati akhīhā qāla lahā akrimī mathwāhā wa-aghnī faqrahā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the chamberlain, when Nuzhat al-Zamān told him the news of her brother's wife, said to her: Honour her lodging, and enrich her poverty.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Nuzhat al-Zamān told the Chamberlain what had befallen her brother's wife, he said to her, “Make her welcome, and see that she wants for nothing.”
sentences.n: The print has فالت, a misprint for قالت, corrected here. The Chamberlain, who has made himself sultan, is Nuzhat al-Zamān's husband; the widow is the mother of Kān Mā Kān, who has been living with them since the last night. akrimī mathwāhā, “make her stay honourable”, repeats his words at the close of the last night, an echo of the Qurʾān (12:21). aghnī faqrahā, “make her poverty rich”: relieve her want.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَزَوْجِهَا وَأُمِّ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri nuzhati al-zamāni wa-zawjihā wa-ummi ḍawʾi al-makāni
sentences.l: This is what was of the affair of Nuzhat al-Zamān and her husband and the mother of Ḍawʾ al-Makān.
sentences.i: So much for Nuzhat al-Zamān, her husband, and Ḍawʾ al-Makān's widow.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for leaving one thread and taking up another: “this is what there was of the matter of …”, then wa-ammā mā kāna min amr …, “and as for what there was of the matter of …”. umm ḍawʾ al-makān, “the mother of Ḍawʾ al-Makān”, must mean his widow, the mother of Kān Mā Kān, and may be a slip for umm kān mā kān; the idiomatic line follows the sense.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَبِنْتِ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ فَإِنَّهُمَا كَبِرَا وَتَرَعْرَعَا حَتَّى صَارَا كَأَنَّهُمَا غُصْنَانِ مُثْمِرَانِ أَوْ قَمَرَانِ أَزْهَرَانِ وَبَلَغَا مِنَ الْعُمْرِ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ عَامًا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri kāna mā kāna wa-binti ʿammihi qaḍā fakāna fa-innahumā kabirā wa-taraʿraʿā ḥattā ṣārā ka-annahumā ghuṣnāni muthmirāni aw qamarāni azharāni wa-balaghā mina al-ʿumri khamsata ʿashara ʿāman
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of Kān Mā Kān and the daughter of his uncle Qaḍā Fakān, they two grew-big and grew-up until they became as-if they were two branches bearing-fruit or two moons shining, and they reached of age fifteen years.
sentences.i: As for Kān Mā Kān and his cousin Qaḍā Fakān, they grew and flourished until they were like two fruitful boughs or two shining moons, and they reached the age of fifteen.
sentences.n: Everything here is in the dual: kabirā, taraʿraʿā, ṣārā, balaghā, “the two of them grew, flourished, became, reached”. taraʿraʿa, “to grow up, shoot up”, is said of a boy or a young plant. bint ʿammihi, “his paternal uncle's daughter”: Qaḍā Fakān is Sharrukān's daughter, Kān Mā Kān is Ḍawʾ al-Makān's son. azhar, “shining, bright”, of the moon.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ قَضَى فَكَانَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الْبَنَاتِ الْمُخَدَّرَاتِ بِوَجْهٍ جَمِيلٍ وَخَدٍّ أَسِيلٍ وَخَصْرٍ نَحِيلٍ وَرِدْفٍ ثَقِيلٍ وَقَدٍّ رَشِيقٍ وَثَغْرٍ أَلَذَّ مِنَ الرَّحِيقِ وَرِيقٍ كَالسَّلْسَبِيلِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا بَعْضُ وَاصِفِيهَا هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat qaḍā fakāna min aḥsani al-banāti al-mukhaddarāti bi-wajhin jamīlin wa-khaddin asīlin wa-khaṣrin naḥīlin wa-ridfin thaqīlin wa-qaddin rashīqin wa-thaghrin aladhdha mina al-raḥīqi wa-rīqin ka-al-salsabīli kamā qāla fīhā baʿḍu wāṣifīhā hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And Qaḍā Fakān was of the most beautiful of the girls the curtained-ones, with a face beautiful, and a cheek smooth-long, and a waist slender, and a buttock heavy, and a stature graceful, and a mouth more-delicious than the choice-wine, and saliva like the Salsabīl, as some of her describers said of her these two lines:
sentences.i: Qaḍā Fakān was among the loveliest of the girls kept behind the curtain: a beautiful face, a long smooth cheek, a slender waist, heavy hips, a graceful figure, a mouth sweeter than the finest wine, and the water of her mouth like Salsabīl, the spring of Paradise, as one who described her said in these two lines:
sentences.n: A run of rhymed pairs: asīl, naḥīl, thaqīl; then rashīq, raḥīq. al-mukhaddarāt, “the curtained ones”, girls kept secluded in the women's quarters (khidr, “curtain”); the print marks the doubled dāl. asīl, of a cheek, “long and smooth”. raḥīq, “choice, pure wine”, the wine of Paradise in the Qurʾān (83:25); Salsabīl is a spring of Paradise (76:18). The print writes aladhdh, “more delicious”, without its hamza and marks the doubled dhāl (الذّ). bi- here is “with”: what she was endowed with.

sentences.t:
كَاَنَّ سُلَافَ الْخَمْرِ مِنْ مَاءِ رِيْقِهَا * وَعُنْقُودُهَا مِنْ ثَغْرِهَا الْعَذْبِ يُقْطَفُ
وَاَعَنَابَهَا مَالَتْ اِذَا مَا ثَنَيْتَهَا * فَسُبْحَانَ خَلَّاقٍ لَهَا لَيْسَ يُوْصَفُ
sentences.tr:
kaʾanna sulāfa al-khamri min māʾi rīqihā * wa-ʿunqūduhā min thaghrihā al-ʿadhbi yuqṭafu
wa-aʿanābahā mālat idhā mā thanaytahā * fa-subḥāna khallāqin lahā laysa yūṣafu
sentences.l:
As-if the first-flow of the wine were from the water of her saliva, * and its cluster from her mouth the sweet is plucked;
and its grapes lean when you bend her: * so glory to a Creator of her who is not described.
sentences.i:
It is as if the first-run wine flowed from the water of her mouth, * as if its cluster were plucked from her sweet lips;
its grapes sway when you bend her to you: * glory, then, to her Maker, past all describing.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -afu, copied as the print points them. sulāf, the juice that runs from the grapes before they are pressed, the finest wine. The print points the opening of the second line wa-aʿanābahā, which is not a correct form; the sense wants wa-aʿnābuhā, “and its grapes”, carrying on the wine, and the print's marks there are hard to read. thanaytahā, “you bend her”, as one bends a branch. khallāq, “Creator”, an intensive form of khāliq. laysa yūṣafu, “is not (to be) described”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ جَمَعَ اللّٰهُ تَعَالَى فِيهَا كُلَّ الْمَحَاسِنِ فَقَدُّهَا يُخْجِلُ الْأَغْصَانَ وَالْوَرْدُ يَطْلُبُ مِنْ خَدِّهَا الْأَمَانَ وَأَمَّا الرِّيقُ فَإِنَّهُ يَهْزَأُ بِالرَّحِيقِ تَسُرُّ الْقَلْبَ وَالنَّاظِرَ كَمَا قِيلَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad jamaʿa allāhu taʿālā fīhā kulla al-maḥāsini fa-qadduhā yukhjilu al-aghṣāna wa-al-wardu yaṭlubu min khaddihā al-amāna wa-ammā al-rīqu fa-innahu yahzaʾu bi-al-raḥīqi tasurru al-qalba wa-al-nāẓira kamā qīla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And God the Exalted had gathered in her all the beauties: so her stature shames the branches, and the rose seeks from her cheek safe-conduct, and as for the saliva, it mocks at the choice-wine; she gladdens the heart and the beholder, as was said of her — the poet:
sentences.i: God, exalted is He, had gathered every beauty in her: her figure put the branches to shame, the rose begged quarter of her cheek, and the water of her mouth made a mockery of the finest wine. She delighted heart and eye, as the poet said of her:
sentences.n: The print has ابالرحيق, with a stray alif, a misprint for بالرحيق, corrected here; hazaʾa bi-, “to mock at”, takes bi- for what is mocked. More rhyme: aghṣān, amān. al-amān, “safety, quarter”, what a defeated enemy asks for. The print marks the doubled dāl of qadd and the doubled rāʾ of tasurru. kamā qīla fīhā al-shāʿiru, “as was said of her — the poet”, does not hang together: the usual phrase is kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿir, “as the poet said of her”, and qīla, “it was said”, may be a slip for qāla, but it is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
مَلِيْحَةُ الْوَصْفِ قَدْ تَمَّتْ مَحَاسِنُهَا * اَجْفَانُهَا تَفْضَحُ التَّكْحِيْلَ بِالْكُحَلِ
كَاَنَّ الْحَاظَهَا فِي قَلْبِ عَاشِقِهَا * سَيْفُ بِكَفِّ اَمِيْرِ الْمُؤْمِنِيْنَ عَلِيْ
sentences.tr:
malīḥatu al-waṣfi qad tammat maḥāsinuhā * ajfānuhā tafḍaḥu al-takḥīla bi-al-kuḥali
kaʾanna alḥāẓahā fī qalbi ʿāshiqihā * sayfu bi-kaffi amīri al-muʾminīna ʿalī
sentences.l:
Lovely of description, her beauties are complete; * her eyelids disgrace the kohl-painting with the natural-dark;
as-if her glances in the heart of her lover * (were) a sword in the palm of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī.
sentences.i:
Lovely past describing, her beauty made complete, * her eyelids, dark by nature, put all painted kohl to shame;
her glances in her lover's heart are like * a sword in the hand of ʿAlī, Commander of the Faithful.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre basīṭ, copied as the print points them. kuḥal, as pointed here, stands for kaḥal, the natural darkness of the eyelid's rim that makes kohl needless; takḥīl is the painting of it. alḥāẓ, “glances”, is printed without its hamza. The print gives sayfu without tanwīn. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the Prophet's cousin and the fourth caliph, is the proverbial swordsman of Islam.

sentences.t: قَالَ الرَّاوِي وَأَمَّا كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ بَدِيعَ الْجَمَالِ فَائِقَ الْكَمَالِ لَيْسَ لَهُ فِى الْوَصْفِ وَالْحُسْنِ مِثَالٌ تَلُوحُ الشَّجَاعَةُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَتَشْهَدُ لَهُ وَلَا تَشْهَدُ عَلَيْهِ وَتَمِيلُ الْقُلُوبُ الْقَاسِيَةُ إِلَيْهِ أَكْحَلُ الطَّرْفِ كَامِلُ الْوَصْفِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-rāwī wa-ammā kāna mā kāna fa-innahu kāna badīʿa al-jamāli fāʾiqa al-kamāli laysa lahu fī al-waṣfi wa-al-ḥusni mithālun talūḥu al-shajāʿatu bayna ʿaynayhi wa-tashhadu lahu wa-lā tashhadu ʿalayhi wa-tamīlu al-qulūbu al-qāsiyatu ilayhi akḥalu al-ṭarfi kāmilu al-waṣfi
sentences.l: The narrator said: And as for Kān Mā Kān, he was wonderful of beauty, surpassing of perfection; there was not for him in description and beauty a likeness; the courage shows between his two eyes, and testifies for him and does not testify against him, and the hearts the hard incline to him; dark-lidded of the eye, complete of description.
sentences.i: The narrator said: As for Kān Mā Kān, he was wonderfully handsome and surpassing in every perfection, with no equal in looks or in beauty. Courage shone between his eyes and spoke for him, never against him, and even hard hearts were drawn to him. His eyes were dark-lidded, and every trait in him was complete.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose again: jamāl, kamāl, mithāl; ʿaynayhi, ʿalayhi, ilayhi; ṭarf, waṣf. qāla al-rāwī, “the narrator said”, is the storyteller's own voice breaking through Shahrazād's. shahida li- / ʿalā, “to testify for / against”. akḥal, “dark-rimmed (of the eyelids)”, a mark of beauty in a young man as in a girl.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اخْضَرَّ شَارِبُهُ وَصَارَ لَهُ عِذَارٌ كَثُرَتْ فِيهِ الْأَشْعَارُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ikhḍarra shāribuhu wa-ṣāra lahu ʿidhārun kathurat fīhi al-ashʿāru
sentences.l: And when his moustache grew-green and there came to be for him a cheek-down, the poems about him became many.
sentences.i: And when his moustache darkened on his lip and the down came on his cheek, poems about him multiplied,
sentences.n: ikhḍarra, “to become green”: Arabic calls the first dark down on a youth's lip and cheek “green”. ʿidhār, the line of down along the cheek, is the favourite subject of the love poetry that follows; the poems are quoted at once, without an introducing phrase.

sentences.t:
مَا بَانَ عُذْرِيْ فِيْهِ حَتَّى عَذَّرَا * وَمَشَى الدُّجَى فِيْ خَدِّهِ فَتَحَيَّرَا
رَشَاءُ اِذَا رَنَتِ الْعُيُوْنُ لِحُسْنِهِ * سَلَّتْ لَوَحِظُهُ عَلَيْهَا خَنْجَرًا
sentences.tr:
mā bāna ʿudhrī fīhi ḥattā ʿadhdharā * wa-mashā al-dujā fī khaddihi fa-taḥayyarā
rashāʾu idhā ranati al-ʿuyūnu li-ḥusnihi * sallat lawaḥiẓuhu ʿalayhā khanjarā
sentences.l:
My excuse in him did not appear until he grew-cheek-down, * and the darkness walked on his cheek and was bewildered;
a fawn: when the eyes gaze at his beauty, * his glances draw against them a dagger.
sentences.i:
My excuse for loving him was never plain until the down came on his cheek, * and the dark walked there, and lost its way;
a fawn: when eyes are fixed upon his beauty, * his glances draw a dagger on them.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -rā, copied as the print points them. A play on words: ʿudhr, “excuse”, and ʿadhdhara, “to grow the cheek-down (ʿidhār)”: only when the down came did the lover's passion seem excusable to others. dujā, “darkness”, is the down again. The print writes rashāʾu (as if “well-rope”); the sense is rashaʾ, “a fawn”, the usual image for a beautiful youth. lawaḥiẓ is printed without its long alif: lawāḥiẓ, “the corners of the eyes, glances”. ranā li-, “to gaze at”.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the saying of the other:
sentences.i: And another poet says:
sentences.n: Short for wa-min dhālika qawlu al-ākhar, “and among them is the saying of another”. The print writes al-ākhar with its own madda (الآخر).

sentences.t:
نَسَخَتْ نُفُوْسُ الْعَاشِقِيْنَ بِخَدِّهِ * نَمْلًا وَتَمَّ بِهَا النَّجِيْعُ الْاَحْمَرُ
فَاعْجَبْ لَهُمْ شَهْدًا وَمَسْكَنُهُمْ لَظَى * وَلِبَاسُهُمْ فِيْهَا الْحَرِيْرُ الْاَخْضَرُ
sentences.tr:
nasakhat nufūsu al-ʿāshiqīna bi-khaddihi * namlan wa-tamma bihā al-najīʿu al-aḥmaru
fa-iʿjab lahum shahdan wa-maskanuhum laẓā * wa-libāsuhum fīhā al-ḥarīru al-akhḍaru
sentences.l:
The souls of the lovers copied on his cheek * ants, and completed with them was the blood the red;
so marvel at them — honey(?) — and their dwelling is Laẓā, * and their clothing in it the silk the green.
sentences.i:
The souls of his lovers have written ants upon his cheek, * and their red blood finished the writing;
marvel at them, then, martyrs whose dwelling is the Blaze, * yet their clothing there is the green silk of Paradise.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -aru, copied as the print points them. naml, “ants”: the fine down on the cheek is likened to a trail of ants, or to small black script, and nasakha, “to copy out”, keeps the writing image. najīʿ, “blood”: the red of his cheek is the blood of the lovers who died of him. The print points shahdan, “honey”; the sense seems to want shuhadāʾ, “martyrs”, which makes the paradox of the line: Laẓā is a name of Hell (Qurʾān 70:15), here the fire of his cheek, yet those who live in it wear the green silk the Qurʾān gives the blessed (18:31). The reading is uncertain, and the literal line keeps the print.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَعْيَادِ أَنَّ قَضَى فَكَانَ خَرَجَتْ تَتَعَيَّدُ عَلَى بَعْضِ أَقَارِبِهَا مِنَ الدَّوْلَةِ وَالْجَوَارِي حَوَالَيْهَا وَالْحُسْنُ قَدْ عَمَّهَا وَرْدُ الْخَدِّ يَحْسُدُ خَالَهَا وَالْأُقْحُوَانُ يَتَبَسَّمُ عَنْ بَارِقِ ثَغْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa fī baʿḍi al-aʿyādi anna qaḍā fakāna kharajat tataʿayyadu ʿalā baʿḍi aqāribihā mina al-dawlati wa-al-jawārī ḥawālayhā wa-al-ḥusnu qad ʿammahā wardu al-khaddi yaḥsudu khālahā wa-al-uqḥuwānu yatabassamu ʿan bāriqi thaghrihā
sentences.l: And it chanced on one of the feasts that Qaḍā Fakān went out keeping-the-feast upon (= visiting) some of her relatives of the state, and the slave-girls around her, and the beauty had covered her; the rose of the cheek envies her mole, and the camomile smiles from the lightning of her mouth.
sentences.i: It happened on a feast day that Qaḍā Fakān went out to pay her festival visit to some of her kinsfolk at court, with her slave-girls about her. Beauty covered her from head to foot; the rose of her cheek envied her beauty-spot, and the camomile flower smiled out from the flash of her teeth.
sentences.n: taʿayyada ʿalā, “to make one's feast-day visit to”, a usage of the spoken language. min al-dawla, “of the state”: of the ruling house and the court. khāl, “mole, beauty-spot”. uqḥuwān, the camomile, whose white-petalled flower is the stock image for teeth; bāriq, “flashing”, the gleam of her teeth when she smiles. The print marks the doubled yāʾ of tataʿayyadu, the doubled mīm of ʿammahā and the doubled sīn of yatabassamu. wardu al-khaddi begins a new clause without wa-.

sentences.t: فَجَعَلَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَدُورُ حَوْلَهَا وَيُطْلِقُ النِّظَارَ إِلَيْهَا وَهِيَ كَالْقَمَرِ الزَّاهِرِ فَقَوَّى جَنَانَهُ وَأَطْلَقَ بِالشِّعْرِ لِسَانَهُ فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-jaʿala kāna mā kāna yadūru ḥawlahā wa-yuṭliqu al-niẓāra ilayhā wa-hiya ka-al-qamari al-zāhiri fa-qawwā janānahu wa-aṭlaqa bi-al-shiʿri lisānahu fa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān began to circle around her and to let loose the looking at her, and she was like the moon the shining; so he strengthened his heart and let loose with the poetry his tongue, and recited, saying:
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān began to hover about her, gazing at her freely, and she was like the shining moon. At last he took heart, loosed his tongue in verse, and recited:
sentences.n: jaʿala with an imperfect, “he began to …”. niẓār, as vocalised here, is a verbal noun of “looking”; the usual phrase is yuṭliqu al-naẓar, “to let one's gaze loose”, and the print's النظار may be a slip for النظر. A rhymed pair: janānahu, lisānahu; janān, “heart, courage”. The print marks the doubled wāw of qawwā. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the regular formula before verse.

sentences.t:
مَتَى يَشْتَفِي قَلْبُ الْكَئِيبِ مِنَ الْبُعْدِ * وَيَضْحَكُ ثَغَرُ الْوَصْلِ مِنْ زَائِلِ الصَّدِّ
فَيَا لَيْتَ شِعْرِي هَلْ اَبِيتَنَّ لَيْلَةً * بِوَصْلِ حَبِيبٍ عِنْدَهُ بَعْضُ مَا عِنْدِي
sentences.tr:
matā yashtafī qalbu al-kaʾībi mina al-buʿdi * wa-yaḍḥaku thagharu al-waṣli min zāʾili al-ṣaddi
fa-yā layta shiʿrī hal abītanna laylatan * bi-waṣli ḥabībin ʿindahu baʿḍu mā ʿindī
sentences.l:
When will the heart of the sorrowful be healed of the distance, * and the mouth of union laugh at the passing of the turning-away?
So O would that my knowing: shall I surely spend a night * in the union of a beloved with whom is some of what is with me?
sentences.i:
When will the grieving heart be cured of distance, * and union's lips smile when coldness has passed?
Would that I knew whether I shall spend one night * in the arms of a love who feels some part of what I feel.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -dī, copied as the print points them; the print points thagharu with two fatḥas for thaghru, “mouth”. ṣadd, “turning away, coldness”, the beloved's refusal. yā layta shiʿrī, “would that my knowledge (were)”, is the fixed phrase “I wish I knew”. abītanna, “I shall surely spend the night”, with the emphatic -anna.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ قَضَي فَكَانَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ أَظْهَرَتْ لَهُ الْمَلَامَةَ وَالْعِتَابَ وَشَمَخَتْ شَمْخَةً فَاغْتَاظَتْ بِكَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَتَذْكُرُنِي فِي شِعْرِكَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تَفْضَحَنِي بَيْنَ أَهْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat qaḍā fakāna hādhihi al-abyāta aẓharat lahu al-malāmata wa-al-ʿitāba wa-shamakhat shamkhatan fa-ightāẓat bi-kāna mā kāna wa-qālat lahu a-tadhkurunī fī shiʿrika li-ajli an tafḍaḥanī bayna ahlika
sentences.l: And when Qaḍā Fakān heard these lines, she showed him the blame and the reproach, and she grew-haughty a haughtiness, and was enraged with Kān Mā Kān, and said to him: Do you mention me in your poetry for the sake of that you disgrace me among your family?
sentences.i: When Qaḍā Fakān heard these lines she let him see her displeasure and reproach. She drew herself up in pride, flew into a rage at Kān Mā Kān, and said to him, “Do you name me in your verses to shame me before your family?
sentences.n: The print spells her name here with a dotted yāʾ (قضي); it is read Qaḍā as everywhere else. shamakha, “to be lofty, carry one's nose high”, with its own verbal noun as object, shamkhatan: “she gave a haughty toss of the head”. ightāẓa, “to be enraged”, here takes bi- for the one she is angry with; ʿalā would be more usual. The question starts with a-, the particle that asks.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ إِنْ لَمْ تَرْجِعْ عَنْ هٰذَا الْمَقَالِ لَأَ شْكِيَنَّكَ لِلْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ سُلْطَانِ خُرَاسَانَ وَبَغْدَادَ صَاحِبِ الْعَدْلِ وَالْإِنْصَافِ يُنْزِلُ بِكَ الذُّلَّ وَالْهَوَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-allāhi in lam tarjiʿ ʿan hādhā al-maqāli la-ashkiyannaka li-al-ḥājibi al-kabīri sulṭāni khurāsāna wa-baghdāda ṣāḥibi al-ʿadli wa-al-inṣāfi yunzilu bika al-dhulla wa-al-hawāna
sentences.l: By God, if you do not turn back from this saying, I shall surely complain of you to the Great Chamberlain, the sultan of Khurāsān and Baghdad, the possessor of the justice and the equity; he will bring down on you the abasement and the contempt.
sentences.i: By God, if you do not leave off this talk, I will complain of you to the Great Chamberlain, Sultan of Khurāsān and Baghdad, the lord of justice and fair dealing, and he will bring shame and contempt down on your head.”
sentences.n: la-ashkiyannaka, “I will surely complain of you”, oath-answer with la- and the emphatic -anna. The print splits it in two (لا شكينك) and builds it on a spoken present ashkī for Classical ashkū, from shakā, “to complain”. The rest rhymes: Khurāsān, hawān. yunzilu bika, “he brings down upon you”: bi- marks the one it falls on.

sentences.t: فَسَكَتَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَاغْتَاظَ وَعَادَ إِلَي بَغْدَادَ وَهُوَ غَضْبَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-sakata kāna mā kāna wa-ightāẓa wa-ʿāda ilā baghdāda wa-huwa ghaḍbānu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān fell silent, and was enraged, and returned to Baghdad, and he was angry.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said nothing, but he was furious, and he went back to Baghdad in anger.
sentences.n: The print writes ilā with a dotted yāʾ (الي), its regular habit. ghaḍbān, “angry”, the adjective of state.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَلَعَتْ قَضَي فَكَانَ إِلَى قَصْرِهَا وَشَكَتْ مِنِ ابْنِ عَمِّهَا إِلَى أُمِّهَا
sentences.tr: thumma ṭalaʿat qaḍā fakāna ilā qaṣrihā wa-shakat mini ibni ʿammihā ilā ummihā
sentences.l: Then Qaḍā Fakān went up to her palace and complained of the son of her uncle to her mother.
sentences.i: Then Qaḍā Fakān went back up to her palace and complained of her cousin to her mother.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, is used in the spoken language for going home to one's quarters. shakā min … ilā, “to complain of … to”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا بِنْتِي لَعَلَّهُ مَا أَرَادَكِ بِسُوءٍ وَهَلْ هُوَإِلَّا يَتِيمٌ وَمَعَ هٰذَا لَمْ يَذْكُرْ شَيْأً يَعِيبُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā yā bintī laʿallahu mā arādaki bi-sūʾin wa-hal huwa illā yatīmun wa-maʿa hādhā lam yadhkur shayʾan yaʿībuki
sentences.l: And she said to her: O my daughter, perhaps he did not intend you with evil; and is he anything but an orphan? And with this, he did not mention a thing that shames you.
sentences.i: Her mother said to her, “My daughter, perhaps he meant you no harm. What is he, after all, but an orphan? Besides, he said nothing that could shame you.
sentences.n: arāda bi-, “to intend (something) towards someone”: bi-sūʾ, “with harm”. hal huwa illā …, “is he anything but …?”; the print runs huwa and illā together (هوالّا) and marks the doubled lām. shayʾ is spelt شيأ, with its hamza on an alif, as the print often has it.

sentences.t: فَإِيَّاكِ أَنْ تُعْلِمِي بِذٰلِكَ أَحَدًا فَإِنَّهُ رُبَّمَا بَلَغَ الْخَبَرُ إِلَى السُّلْطَانِ فَيُقَصِّرُ عُمْرَهُ وَيُخْمِدُ ذِكْرَهُ وَيَجْعَلُهُ كَأَمْسِ مَضَي ذِكْرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-iyyāki an tuʿlimī bi-dhālika aḥadan fa-innahu rubbamā balagha al-khabaru ilā al-sulṭāni fa-yuqaṣṣiru ʿumrahu wa-yukhmidu dhikrahu wa-yajʿaluhu ka-amsi maḍā dhikruhu
sentences.l: So beware of informing anyone of that, for perhaps the news would reach the sultan, and he would cut-short his life and extinguish his memory and make him like yesterday whose mention has passed.
sentences.i: Take care not to tell anyone of it, for the news might reach the Sultan, and he would cut his life short, blot out his name and make him like yesterday, gone and forgotten.”
sentences.n: iyyāki an …, “beware of …”. aʿlama bi-, “to inform (someone) of”: bi- marks the thing told. Rhyme again: ʿumrahu, dhikrahu, and dhikruhu at the close. ka-amsi maḍā, “like a yesterday that has passed”, a stock phrase for what is utterly gone. The print writes maḍā with a dotted yāʾ (مضي).

sentences.t: هٰذَاوَشَاعَ فِي بَغْدَادَ حُبُّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لِقَضَى فَكَانَ وَتَحَدَّثَتْ بِهِ النِّسْوَانُ
sentences.tr: hādhā wa-shāʿa fī baghdāda ḥubbu kāna mā kāna li-qaḍā fakāna wa-taḥaddathat bihi al-niswānu
sentences.l: This; and there spread in Baghdad the love of Kān Mā Kān for Qaḍā Fakān, and the women talked of it.
sentences.i: So it was. And word spread through Baghdad of Kān Mā Kān's love for Qaḍā Fakān, and the women talked of it.
sentences.n: hādhā, “this (is how it was)”, closes the scene, and the print runs it into the next word (هذاوشاع). ḥubb … li-, “love for”: li- marks the one loved. taḥaddatha bi-, “to talk about”. niswān, a plural of imraʾa, “woman”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ ضَاقَ صَدْرُهُ وَعِيلَ صَبْرُهُ وَقَلَّ حَيْلُهُ وَلَمْ يَخْفَ عَلَي النَّاسِ حَالُهُ وَاشْتَهَى أَنْ يَبُوحَ بِمَا فِي قَلْبِهِ مِنْ لَوْعَةِ الْبَيْنِ فَخَافَ مِنْ عَتْبِهَا وَغَضَبِهَا فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna kāna mā kāna ḍāqa ṣadruhu wa-ʿīla ṣabruhu wa-qalla ḥayluhu wa-lam yakhfa ʿalā al-nāsi ḥāluhu wa-ishtahā an yabūḥa bi-mā fī qalbihi min lawʿati al-bayni fa-khāfa min ʿatbihā wa-ghaḍabihā fa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān, his breast became narrow, and his patience was exhausted, and his strength became little, and his state was not hidden from the people; and he desired to disclose what was in his heart of the burning of the separation, but he feared her reproach and her anger, so he recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān grew heavy-hearted; his patience was spent, his strength failed, and his condition was no secret to anyone. He longed to speak out the pain of parting that burned in his heart, but he feared her reproach and her anger, and he recited:
sentences.n: More rhyme: ṣadruhu, ṣabruhu; ḥayluhu, ḥāluhu. ḍāqa ṣadruhu, “his breast grew narrow”: he was distressed. ʿīla ṣabruhu, “his patience was overcome”. ḥayl, “strength, power”. The print writes ʿalā with a dotted yāʾ (علي) and marks the doubled lām of qalla. bāḥa bi-, “to disclose”: bi- marks the secret. lawʿa, “the burning pain” of love; bayn, “separation”.

sentences.t:
اِذَا خِفْتُ يَوْمًا عِتَابَ الَّتِيْ * تَكَدَّرَ اَخْلَاقَهَا الصَّافِيَهْ
صَبَرْتُ عَلَيْهَا كَصَبْرِ الْفَتَى * عَلَى الْكَيِّ فِيْ طَلَبِ الْعَافِيَهْ
sentences.tr:
idhā khiftu yawman ʿitāba allatī * takaddara akhlāqahā al-ṣāfiyah
ṣabartu ʿalayhā ka-ṣabri al-fatā * ʿalā al-kayyi fī ṭalabi al-ʿāfiyah
sentences.l:
When I fear one day the reproach of her whose * clear nature has become-clouded,
I am patient with her like the patience of the young-man * under the cautery in seeking of health.
sentences.i:
If ever I fear the reproach of her * whose clear temper clouds over,
I bear it as a young man bears * the cautery, for the sake of his cure.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre mutaqārib, rhyming in -iyah, copied as the print points them. The print points takaddara akhlāqahā, which does not construe; the sense is takaddarat akhlāquhā, “whose clear manners grow clouded”. kayy, cauterising with a hot iron, was a regular cure: the pain is borne for the healing. The rhyme words end in a pausal -ah, which the print marks with sukūn.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The print sets Shahrazād's name in two words here (شهر زاد).
